transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-08-29
Start: 14:30 PDT
Duration: ~52 mins
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Ross (Redwood SE), Dr. Miguel Santos (CISO - Halcyon), Aisha Khan (Head Eng), Liam O'Connor (Compliance), Priya Iyer (Product)

Auto-summary (auto gen): Health care provider exploring Redwood hosting options for ePHI workloads, primary ask HIPAA + EU residency interplay.

[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Samira from Redwood, with Ethan our solutions engineer. Quick sanity check on the agenda—cover our hosting paths and then dig into keys, logs, and residency questions.
[00:18] Miguel: Yep, that's great. I'm Miguel, CISO at Halcyon. We, um, primarily want to understand where patient data sits and what control we have over keys. Also, interface with our EU partners — some of our cohorts are in the EU and we need to honor subject requests.
[00:34] Ethan: Totally. We'll walk through Hosted API, Dedicated, and Private (VPC/on-prem) and tradeoffs. Quick note though, sometimes our hosted offering gets called "Redwood hosted" or "Hosted API" but some of the docs say Redwood cloud — apologies if naming mismatch in the deck.
[00:48] Aisha: One minute — are you able to confirm if hosted can be configured to only store logs in EU regions?
[00:54] Samira: Short answer: yes, region locking for logs is supported for customers on enterprise plan, we can configure log sinks to EU regions. For ePHI we recommend Dedicated or Private, but hosted is possible with the right data-flow controls.
[01:12] Liam: When you say "we can configure" — is that tenant-level or request-level? We need proof for auditors that log transmissions never leave EU control plane for EU patients.
[01:23] Ethan: Good question. For hosted we can do region pinning for the control plane and also configure retention policies so logs are stored in EU buckets. It's an opt-in in the platform console — the control plane is multi-region but you can lock to an EU control plane for an account. Although, caveat, some metadata used for routing may still cross borders unless you choose a Private deployment.
[01:46] Priya: That's the sort of nuance we need, because our legal team cares about even ephemeral metadata.
[01:51] Samira: Understood. On that front, Private gives you customer-managed control plane and private networking — so no routing metadata leaves your VPC. Dedicated is in-between: dedicated GPU pools and tenancy, with stronger isolation and the option to have the control plane in a specific region, but control plane is still Redwood-managed unless you go Private.
[02:12] Miguel: And for keys — we need BYOK with HSM-backed keys, and ideally key lifecycle audits and ability to rotate without downtime.
[02:22] Ethan: We support BYOK with HSM-backed keys. You can bring keys via cloud KMS or an on-prem HSM. Rotation can be configured with a staged roll (we do key-rolling of the model envelope keys + ephemeral tokens) — there is a short handover but it shouldn't cause generation failures. We'll share a runbook.
[02:39] Aisha: Does BYOK mean logs might still contain unencrypted payloads? We're trying to avoid any ePHI ever landing in plaintext in logs.
[02:49] Ethan: Right — by default some logs may include request/response snippets for debugging. For HIPAA workloads we recommend log redaction and tokenization. Platform supports redaction rules (regex-based) and we can disable content logging entirely for high-sensitivity routes. There are three modes: full logging off, sanitized logging (pii redaction), and full logging with encryption-at-rest only.
[03:10] Liam: Can you show an example redaction rule?
[03:14] Samira: We'll include sample regex set in the follow-up. Off the cuff: a rule to strip sequences matching health id patterns, SSNs, dates tied to patient id etc — but we'll need your classification patterns.
[03:25] Miguel: We'll send a sample of classification. Do you provide audit logs that show who accessed an inference request and which key version was used?
[03:33] Ethan: Yes. Audit trails show request id, model variant, key id, token issuer and service principal, and action (create/generate/revoke). Keep in mind the audit events are separate from content logs — so they show metadata about the call but not the ePHI content if redaction is enabled.
[03:52] Priya: There's an EU angle — if a patient requests data deletion under GDPR, how do you map that to logs and model caches? We have models that cache prefixes for speed.
[04:03] Ethan: Two parts: KV/prefix caches and logs. For caches we have per-tenant TTL and can selectively evict keys. If a deletion request comes in, we can map associated cache keys to the user and evict — but you'll need mapping metadata on your side to link user identifiers to cache keys. For model outputs persisted externally (e.g., embeddings) you'd have to delete those objects from storage. We'll share our eviction API.
[04:29] Miguel: Interesting. And regarding backups and legal hold — auditors may demand that certain records can't be deleted for a fixed period; can you enforce legal hold to prevent cache eviction?
[04:38] Ethan: We support legal hold flags on tenant data, but for ePHI you'll typically configure your retention policies centrally. Legal hold will prevent automated deletion; manual processes are required to lift it. We'll include a diagram of retention vs hold behavior.
[04:55] Aisha: From a latency standpoint, Dedicated is appealing — we need sub-150ms 95th for our triage microservice. Have you published benchmarks for that?
[05:03] Samira: We have verified performance profiles per model; Dedicated with pinned GPU pools and continuous batching usually hits those latencies depending on prompt length. Ethan can share a model-by-model latency matrix and we'll run a 100-rps baseline as an action item.
[05:19] Ethan: I'll set up a quick benchmark on our end — but your prompt lengths and max tokens matter. Also, batching can increase throughput but might add tail latency so we can tailor autoscale and batching policies.
[05:33] Liam: Security certifications — we need SOC 2 Type II and ISO evidence for the hosted option.
[05:39] Samira: We are SOC 2 Type II; we'll attach the report to the hub link. For EU residency, we also maintain region-specific attestations and can supply encrypt-at-rest evidence, pen-test summaries, and our incident response playbook.
[05:53] Miguel: Anything about breach notification timelines? We have contractual 72-hour notification obligations.
[05:58] Samira: Standard is 72 hours for confirmed incidents; we'll quote it in the security pack. For Dedicated customers we can add shorter contractual SLAs if needed.
[06:08] Priya: A quick question on model versions: We want to pin a version for production and control rollouts. How are A/B rollouts handled in Dedicated vs Hosted?
[06:16] Ethan: Same API surface — you can pin model versions, do canary rollouts, A/B splits. In Hosted it's managed, in Dedicated you have the same capabilities but the underlying resource pool is reserved, which gives deterministic performance during rollouts. Private gives you full control but you'd manage the underlying infra.
[06:36] Miguel: From compliance — if our researchers in the EU want to run small fine-tunes on de-identified data, can we do that in Redwood or do we need Private?
[06:45] Ethan: Fine-tuning with ePHI de-identified can be done on Dedicated with proper controls. For strictly regulated datasets we recommend Private or an on-prem package. Also note: some fine-tune artifacts and training logs may travel to the control plane unless you use Private.
[06:59] Aisha: Are there custom contract addenda for data residency and restricted access?
[07:03] Samira: Yes — we do addenda for residency, restricted access, and SSO/SAML integrations. For SSO we support SAML2.0 and OIDC and RBAC with fine-grained roles.
[07:15] Liam: Do you have role provisioning connectors for SCIM?
[07:19] Ethan: Yep, SCIM provisioning. We also support SCIM groups mapped to RBAC roles which helps automate deprovs.
[07:30] Miguel: One more thorny issue — cross-border support for data subject access requests (DSARs). If an EU patient asks for all records, and some processing happened in the US, how do we prove that we've served the request correctly?
[07:43] Ethan: Best practice is to keep a dual-track: replicate metadata and audit evidence in the EU tenant account (read-only replica) and have content kept in EU buckets. For DSARs you can query the EU-scope audit logs. We'll put together an example DSAR workflow that maps request IDs to audit entries and cache eviction steps.
[08:03] Priya: That would be great — it's the single biggest blocker for our legal team.
[08:07] Samira: Ok, recap and next steps: we'll send HIPAA architecture notes, the SOC2 artifact, a sample redaction regex pack, the eviction API doc, and Ethan will run the latency/cost baseline. We'll also schedule a finance walkthrough for Dedicated pricing.
[08:24] Miguel: Sounds good. Any quick ask from us?
[08:27] Samira: If you can share your data classification sample and an example retention requirement (e.g., 7 years for certain records) that'll help us draft a config proposal.
[08:36] Miguel: We'll send that by next Friday.
[08:39] Ethan: One small note — for Hosted customers we sometimes recommend tokenization on ingestion to minimize ePHI in transit. It's an extra layer but can reduce audit surface.
[08:50] Aisha: We'll include that in the classification doc.
[08:54] Samira: Great. Thanks all, we'll follow up with the artifacts.
[08:58] (general thanks, meeting ends)

Notes on transcript quality: Automated transcript had a few mis-heard technical words (e.g., "control plane" sometimes transcribed as "control plain") and a couple of names were misattributed, please refer to attendees list for canonical names.
